name: Aceh
summary_text: Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Aceh operates inside that national framework rather than alongside it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.  Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.  Aceh is the only province in Indonesia operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). Same-sex conduct falls under the headings liwath and musahaqah.  Public caning is the standing punishment for sharia offences in Aceh. On 26 August 2025 two men were publicly caned in the provincial capital after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Two men were also publicly caned in the province in February 2025 for a same-sex relationship.  Physical risk extends beyond the courts. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.  Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.  Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.  Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.  Documents and status are restrictive. Indonesia recognises only male and female sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

sources.title: Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI) Fatwa - March 2015
sources.documents: Religious-legal pressure: declares homosexuality curable disease, calls for same-sex acts to be punished by caning and in some instances death penalty; cited as moral guidance not positive law.
sources.detail: Cited as 'In March 2015, Indonesian Ulema Council (Majelis Ulama Indonesia or MUI) issued a fatwa... called for same-sex acts to be punished by caning, and in some instances, the death penalty.' Plus DPR response that fatwa only serves as moral guidance. No URL visible.

sources.title: Constitutional Court of Indonesia Decision - 14 December 2017 (5-4)
sources.documents: National court ruling on criminalization attempt: rejected Family Love Alliance petition to erase 'underage' in Article 292 and amend Articles 248, 285, 292 to criminalize gay sex and sex outside marriage; held issue for legislature.
sources.detail: Cited as 'On 14 December 2017, the Constitutional Court... issued a 5-4 ruling rejecting a petition... sought to erase the term "underage" in article 292, in order to persecute all same-sex sexual conducts.' No URL visible.

sources.title: Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar case - legal gender recognition precedent
sources.documents: Trans rights machinery: first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female; establishes court-approved legal gender change after sex reassignment surgery and judge approval, enabling opposite-legal-gender marriage.
sources.detail: Cited as 'cases like Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar (the first trans Indonesian to be legally recognized as female) giving rise to legal recognition of trans Indonesians' actual genders by the State' and 'allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and after receiving a judge's approval.' No URL visible.

sources.documents: Rights-protection machinery: police duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation; 2015 circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity; constitutional/human-rights law theoretical employment discrimination protection.

name: West Papua
summary_text: West Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, add their own criminalisation, but West Papua is not among them.  The dominant risk in this province is the conduct of the security forces rather than any trans-specific provision. A report of 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network records 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua, covering the period through early 2025. Most victims were male and under 24; seven were female, seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The report's finding is near-total impunity, summarised as impunity, secrecy and silence. Any visitor held or questioned by officers in the province faces an accountability environment in which abuse is unlikely to be answered for.  Military activity in the province has intensified. The Papua human-rights monitor's quarterly report for the third quarter of 2025 records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. Police in Sorong arrested more than a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.  No trans-specific finding is recorded for West Papua in these sources. The general security-force pattern nonetheless amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, since stops, document checks and detention in the province are handled by units already documented committing ill-treatment with impunity.

sources.title: Indonesian Penal Code (KUHP) - 2022 revision, in force 2 January 2026
sources.documents: National legal status applicable in West Papua: sex outside marriage punishable up to 1 year on family complaint; spokesperson and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stated it does not criminalize private LGBTQ orientation, only same-sex sexual violence/rape of minors and public immoral acts; draft Art.421(1) on same-sex obscenity in public (1.5 years).
sources.detail: No URL visible in excerpt; cited as December 2022 Parliament bill, Art.248 adultery, Art.285 rape, Art.292 child abuse, Art.421(1) obscenity, effective date 2 January 2026
